390910.long_answer: An axillary lymph node that is 13 mm in size and lacks a fatty hilum is a nonspecific imaging finding. While loss of the fatty hilum can raise suspicion for a variety of malignant or inflammatory processes (e.g., metastatic carcinoma, lymphoma, reactive hyperplasia), it is not characteristic or diagnostic for the rare hematologic malignancy T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL). T-PLL is usually identified through marked peripheral blood lymphocytosis, splenomegaly, and generalized lymphadenopathy confirmed by immunophenotyping of circulating T-cells—not by the isolated appearance of a single mildly enlarged axillary node on imaging. Therefore, the described node does not specifically suggest T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia.

506648.long_answer: Maternal pre-gestational diabetes is recognized as a prenatal risk factor for several conotruncal heart defects, but epidemiologic studies consistently show a stronger association with transposition of the great vessels (transposition of the great arteries) than with Tetralogy of Fallot. Reported odds ratios for transposition are generally higher (often ≥3- to 4-fold) than those for Tetralogy of Fallot (approximately 1.5- to 2-fold). Therefore, the magnitude of risk is not considered equal between the two lesions; the association is markedly greater for transposition of the great vessels.

719196.long_answer: Rubella virus is transmitted through respiratory droplets. Infected individuals are considered contagious from roughly 7 days before the appearance of the rash until about 7 days after its onset. The third day of symptoms therefore falls well within this infectious window. A person who lacks immunity (i.e., has neither been vaccinated nor previously infected) and who has close face-to-face contact, such as during a conversation, can inhale these droplets and contract the disease. Consequently, the non-immune individual is indeed at risk of acquiring rubella in this scenario.
